Family Health

Women’s health screening: building a plan at every age

Updated: November 6, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A “complete checkup” is not one universal collection of tests. Useful screening depends on your age, risks, previous results and local health programme. Whether you are planning pregnancy, approaching menopause or looking after your health later in life, the aim is to choose checks that can help you and understand what happens next: not to order everything at once.

Start with your history, not a universal test package

A useful preventive visit considers your age, the organs you have, previous results, medicines, personal and family history, and whether you are pregnant or planning pregnancy. Screening looks for a condition or risk before symptoms appear. Tests for a new symptom, monitoring of an established illness and follow-up of an abnormal result have different purposes and schedules.

Bring previous screening dates and reports, operations, diagnoses, family cancer or fracture history, and a medicine list. Ask which checks are due now and why. An annual preventive visit can help coordinate care; it does not mean that every blood test, scan, pelvic examination or cancer test should be repeated annually. Preconception care is one part of a plan that continues through later life.

Weigh benefits, limits and the next step

Suitable screening can find treatable risks, detect some cancers earlier or identify changes that can be treated before cancer develops. No test guarantees prevention or rules out all illness. A false positive can lead to extra tests and worry; a false negative can miss a problem. Some screening also finds disease that would never have caused harm, leading to unnecessary treatment.

Before agreeing, ask what a result would change, what discomfort or complications are possible, and who will arrange follow-up. Recommendations differ between countries and organisations because tests, evidence, resources and judgments about benefit and harm differ. The US and England examples below are labelled examples, not one worldwide timetable. Personal high-risk or previous-abnormal-result pathways may override routine invitations.

Breast changes and screening examinations are different

Be familiar with what is usual for your breasts and seek assessment for a new lump, nipple or skin change rather than waiting for screening. A clinician may examine a breast because of symptoms or individual risk. That is different from scheduling a clinical breast examination as an automatic screening test for every healthy woman.

The American Cancer Society does not recommend routine clinical breast examinations for average-risk screening at any age. A normal examination is not a substitute for a mammogram when one is indicated. Tell your clinician about previous breast cancer, relevant inherited gene changes, a strong family history or earlier chest radiation; these may require a specialist surveillance plan.

Mammography: use a named programme and your risk

Mammography uses low-dose X-rays to look for breast changes. For average-risk women, the US Preventive Services Task Force recommends screening every two years from 40 through 74. The American Cancer Society offers annual screening as an option at 40–44, recommends it annually at 45–54, and allows every two years or annually from 55 while health and life expectancy support it. These are different recommendations, not appointments to combine.

Mammography can miss cancer and can lead to additional imaging or biopsy when no cancer is present. Discuss discomfort, radiation and overdiagnosis as well as benefit. High-risk people may need MRI alongside mammography and an earlier start. Dense breasts alone do not create a universal instruction for extra ultrasound or MRI; the USPSTF finds the evidence insufficient to recommend for or against supplemental screening on that basis. Older-age decisions also need individual discussion.

Cervical screening: HPV and cell tests have specific intervals

Cervical screening checks a sample from the cervix for high-risk HPV, abnormal cells, or both, depending on the programme and age. HPV is common; a positive screening result does not itself mean cancer. Finding and treating important cell changes can reduce cancer risk. Screening is not a test for every gynaecological cancer and does not replace assessment of symptoms.

In England, routine invitations generally cover ages 25–64 every five years, with earlier follow-up when results or history require it. US guidance uses different starting ages and test-dependent intervals, so use your own service’s schedule. Ask specifically about previous abnormal results, treatment, immune suppression, whether a hysterectomy removed the cervix, or being older without adequate prior screening. Bleeding after sex, between periods or after menopause, or unusual discharge needs assessment without waiting for the next screen.

HPV vaccination and STI testing are separate decisions

HPV vaccination helps prevent new infections; it does not treat an existing infection or replace cervical screening. In the US, routine vaccination is at 11–12 years and can start at 9; catch-up is recommended through 26, while some adults 27–45 may benefit after an individual discussion. Products and programmes vary by country. Tell the service if you are pregnant: remaining doses are usually delayed, but an inadvertently given dose is not a reason for alarm.

A cervical screening sample is not a complete STI check. CDC guidance recommends annual chlamydia and gonorrhoea testing for sexually active women under 25, and for older women with risk factors such as a new or multiple partners. Pregnancy has its own recommended infection tests. Discuss symptoms, exposure sites and partner history privately so the service can select the right urine, swab or blood tests; not everyone needs the same annual panel.

Bone density: assess fracture risk as well as age

Osteoporosis can weaken bones without pain before a fracture. A central DXA scan measures bone mineral density, usually at the hip and spine, and is interpreted with fracture risk. The USPSTF recommends screening women aged 65 or over, and postmenopausal women under 65 who have increased fracture risk after clinical risk assessment. A scan is not automatically needed by every younger person.

An earlier low-trauma fracture, low body weight, early menopause, family history, eating problems, kidney or inflammatory disease, and medicines such as long-term steroids deserve discussion. A previous fragility fracture or a disease or medicine causing bone loss is a separate clinical pathway, not a reason to wait until 65. Results should lead to an appropriate prevention or treatment plan, not an assumption that calcium supplements alone solve the problem.

Skin checks: act on changes, not a blanket annual rule

Risk assessment considers UV exposure, skin characteristics, previous skin cancer and family history; skin cancer can occur in any skin colour. For asymptomatic people at average risk, the USPSTF finds insufficient evidence to establish the benefit–harm balance of routine clinician skin screening. That does not mean suspicious lesions should be ignored or that people with an important history should have no follow-up.

Arrange assessment of a mole changing in shape, border, colour or size, a mole that hurts, itches, bleeds or crusts, or a new unusual mark that persists. An unexplained dark area under a nail also needs checking. Small lesions can matter; do not use a size cut-off or phone photograph to rule out cancer. A specialist may examine the skin closely and remove a suspicious lesion for laboratory testing, called an excision biopsy.

Blood pressure: repeat and confirm appropriately

Blood pressure is written with the systolic pressure first and the diastolic second: 120/80 mmHg is in that order, not reversed. A properly sized cuff, a validated device and correct resting technique matter. One high clinic measurement does not usually establish chronic hypertension; a clinician may confirm it with home readings or an ambulatory monitor. Symptoms, pregnancy or very high readings can require a different response.

As a US example, the USPSTF recommends adult screening from 18, with annual checks for people 40 or over or at increased risk. For low-risk adults 18–39 with a previous normal result, every three to five years may be reasonable. Definitions and treatment thresholds differ between programmes and measurement settings. Ask what your own result means and what follow-up is needed rather than applying a single online “normal” label.

Cholesterol: consider the whole cardiovascular picture

A lipid blood test may report total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, HDL cholesterol and triglycerides. LDL can contribute to arterial plaque, while HDL and the other values help interpret the overall picture; no single number determines treatment for everyone. Age, blood pressure, smoking, diabetes, kidney disease and family history can change the risk discussion and testing frequency.

CDC advice gives every four to six years as an example for many healthy adults, with more frequent testing for higher-risk people. Most routine cholesterol tests do not require fasting, although a service may request it for a particular test or result. Follow the actual instructions rather than fasting automatically. Appropriate food, activity and smoking-cessation support, and sometimes medicine, are considered together; tell the prescriber about pregnancy plans before changing treatment yourself.

Diabetes screening: risk and pregnancy change the plan

A US USPSTF recommendation covers asymptomatic, nonpregnant adults aged 35–70 with overweight or obesity. Other risks can justify earlier testing, including a history of gestational diabetes or a strong family history. A normal result may be repeated after about three years in that programme, but the right interval depends on risk and results. Neither age 35 nor a normal past test is a reason to ignore symptoms.

Possible tests include fasting plasma glucose, HbA1c and an oral glucose tolerance test. Pregnancy uses a separate gestational-diabetes pathway with its own timing and interpretation; do not substitute a routine adult screening schedule for antenatal care. If a test indicates increased diabetes risk, ask about effective support for suitable activity, nutrition and other risk reduction, and when to check again.

Understand glucose tests without diagnosing yourself

HbA1c reflects average blood glucose over roughly the previous three months; it does not measure blood pressure and usually requires no fasting. A fasting plasma glucose test generally requires at least eight hours without food. An oral glucose tolerance test measures glucose after a specified drink and timed blood samples. Follow the service’s preparation instructions, particularly if you take medicines.

For nonpregnant adults, fasting plasma glucose of 100–125 mg/dL is in the prediabetes range and 126 mg/dL or higher is in the diabetes range. These values are not interchangeable with mmol/L or a home meter reading; diagnosis usually needs a confirming test and clinical interpretation. Pregnancy uses different criteria, and anaemia or some haemoglobin conditions can make HbA1c less reliable. Ask which test and units were used rather than treating a highlighted number as a complete diagnosis.

HIV testing: the test type and timing matter

CDC advice includes at least one HIV test for people aged 13–64, repeat testing when risk continues, and testing during each pregnancy. A laboratory antigen–antibody test using blood from a vein can usually detect infection 18–45 days after exposure; other tests have different windows. A negative result too early may need repeating, and medicines used for prevention can change the follow-up plan. A positive screening result requires confirmation.

HIV is not the same as AIDS, and effective treatment can protect health and greatly reduce transmission risk, including through appropriate pregnancy care. Condoms, selected pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) and exposure-specific advice remain relevant. After a possible substantial-risk exposure, seek urgent medical advice immediately about post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP): it should start as soon as possible and no later than 72 hours when indicated. Do not wait for symptoms or the next routine screening date.

Colorectal screening: several methods, with follow-up

Screening can detect some bowel cancers early and identify polyps that can be removed before they become cancer. The USPSTF recommends average-risk screening at 45–75, with individual decisions at 76–85. Examples include a yearly stool FIT test or a colonoscopy every ten years after an appropriate negative examination. Previous polyps, cancer, inflammatory bowel disease or inherited risk change the plan; these routine intervals are not for everyone.

A positive stool screen needs colonoscopy follow-up to obtain the screening benefit; repeating a stool test to avoid that discussion is not a substitute. Colonoscopy requires preparation and may involve sedation, and it can allow polyp removal. Bleeding and bowel perforation are uncommon but important harms to discuss. Screening lowers risk rather than guaranteeing prevention. New bowel symptoms require assessment through the appropriate clinical pathway, even after a recent normal screen.

Glaucoma and eye checks: pressure alone is not enough

Glaucoma damages the optic nerve and may progress without obvious early symptoms. It can occur even when eye pressure is within the usual range. An eye professional considers the optic nerve, visual function and other findings, not just a pressure reading. Discuss family history, age, ancestry, eye injury, long-term steroid use and medical conditions such as diabetes; never stop a prescribed steroid independently.

The USPSTF finds insufficient evidence for population primary-care screening for open-angle glaucoma in asymptomatic adults aged 40 or over. That is a different question from regular comprehensive sight checks: NHS advice generally recommends sight tests at least every two years, with shorter intervals when advised. Use an individual eye-care plan rather than universal age bands copied from a checklist, and have new eye symptoms assessed promptly.

Include mental health in preventive care

A preventive visit is also a place to discuss mood, anxiety, sleep and how you are coping. The USPSTF recommends adult depression screening, including during pregnancy, after birth and in older adulthood, when positive results can be followed by assessment and appropriate care. A questionnaire result is not itself a diagnosis, and normal blood tests do not rule out depression.

Seek help when low mood persists, you lose interest in usual activities or coping becomes difficult; you do not have to wait for a routine screening invitation. If you need urgent mental health support, contact an urgent clinical or crisis service. If someone’s life is at risk or you cannot keep yourself or someone else safe, get emergency help immediately. An evidence gap about population suicide screening does not lessen the importance of actual danger.

Leave with an achievable plan and a results contact

Ask for a written list of what is due, which programme or risk factor supports it, how to prepare and when results should arrive. Mention possible pregnancy, previous difficult examinations, accessibility needs and anything that would make attendance hard. You can ask what will happen during an examination and discuss support or alternatives before consenting. Do not silently repeat a test because an old report is missing; ask whether the record can be obtained.

Agree who will explain each result and what to do if no result arrives. A normal result does not cancel a future symptom; an abnormal screen often needs another step rather than an immediate diagnosis. Ask about costs and help arranging follow-up if these are barriers. Keep future dates alongside any referral or monitoring plan so age-based screening does not displace care already needed for an illness.

Symptoms should not wait for the next screening round

Arrange assessment for a new breast lump or nipple or skin change, unusual vaginal bleeding or discharge, a changing mole, or new bowel symptoms. Eye pain, a red painful eye, light sensitivity, blurred or double vision, flashing lights or a moving dark shadow need urgent assessment. These are reasons for clinical care, not reasons to book a routine screening test and wait.

Get emergency help if you suddenly cannot see from one or both eyes, or have sudden severe eye pain. Sudden glaucoma-type symptoms (such as a red or tender eye, coloured halos, blurred sight, intense eye pain, headache or nausea and vomiting) also need emergency assessment; do not wait for all symptoms together or try to confirm the diagnosis yourself. Do not drive yourself to emergency care: ask someone to take you or call an ambulance. Immediate danger to your own or another person’s safety also needs emergency help.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Bring previous results, family history, medicines and pregnancy plans; ask which screening is due under your local programme and which symptoms need separate assessment.

Ask about benefit, possible harm, preparation, alternatives and follow-up before accepting a test. A preventive visit is not an automatic all-test package.

Keep the results contact and next appointment date. Follow up abnormal findings and seek care for new symptoms even after a normal result.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to organise dates, reports, medicine lists and questions for your next appointment, including who will explain results. It cannot decide which screening programme applies, calculate a diagnosis from a result, examine a lump or eye, or replace a clinician’s risk assessment. Recording a symptom must not delay urgent care.

When to seek help

Screening is for people without the relevant symptoms. Arrange assessment for new breast, bleeding, discharge, skin or bowel changes; get urgent advice for eye pain, a red painful eye, light sensitivity or new visual disturbance. Sudden inability to see or sudden severe eye pain requires emergency care. Sudden glaucoma-type symptoms such as redness or tenderness, halos, blurred sight, intense pain, headache or nausea and vomiting also need emergency assessment without waiting for all signs. Do not drive yourself; arrange another driver or an ambulance. Immediate danger to your own or another person’s safety needs emergency help. A recent possible substantial-risk HIV exposure needs immediate advice about time-sensitive PEP, not a later routine test.

Evidence notes updated: November 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Preventive visits coordinate care; they do not make every blood test, scan or examination an annual requirement.
  • Use your own country’s programme and personal risk assessment. Average-risk schedules do not cover every previous abnormal result or high-risk condition.
  • Cervical screening, HPV vaccination, STI testing and HIV testing have different purposes and timing.
  • Blood pressure, cholesterol, glucose and bone results need interpretation and a follow-up plan; a number alone is not the whole diagnosis.
  • New symptoms need assessment even after normal screening. Sudden vision loss or severe eye pain and immediate safety danger need emergency care.

Frequently asked questions

Which tests belong in a complete women’s checkup?

There is no fixed package for everyone. Review the screening that fits your age, organs, medical and family history, previous results and local programme. Breast, cervical, bone, skin, blood-pressure, lipid, diabetes, HIV, bowel and eye checks may have different indications. A preventive appointment can coordinate them without ordering all of them.

Can cervical screening or the HPV vaccine completely prevent cervical cancer?

They reduce risk but do not provide a guarantee. Vaccination prevents new infections rather than treating existing ones, and appropriate screening is still needed. Follow up an abnormal result. Unusual bleeding or discharge needs assessment even when a previous screen was normal.

When should I ask for a bone-density scan?

The USPSTF recommends screening women from 65 and younger postmenopausal women at increased fracture risk after assessment. A previous low-trauma fracture, relevant disease or long-term steroid treatment can need a separate pathway earlier. Age alone does not decide every person’s need for DXA.

Which mole changes need checking?

Seek assessment for a change in size, shape, border or colour, or a mole that becomes painful, itchy, bleeding or crusted. A persistent unusual new mark or unexplained dark nail area also needs checking. Small size does not rule out melanoma; a specialist decides whether examination or biopsy is needed.

Who is at higher risk of glaucoma?

Family history, age, ancestry, eye injury, long-term steroid use and some eye or medical conditions can increase risk. A pressure-only test cannot rule it out, and normal-range pressure does not exclude it. Ask an eye professional about a complete examination and your follow-up interval.

Do all these blood tests require fasting?

No. HbA1c usually does not, and most routine cholesterol tests do not. Fasting plasma glucose and some other tests do require preparation. Follow the specific laboratory instructions and ask about your medicines rather than fasting or withholding treatment on your own.

Does an abnormal screen mean I have cancer or another disease?

Not necessarily. Screening identifies people who may need more assessment. Ask what confirmation or follow-up is needed and how quickly. A positive stool screen, for example, needs the recommended colonoscopy discussion; a normal screen also cannot explain away a new symptom.

Why do mammogram ages differ between guidelines?

Organisations can weigh the benefits and harms differently. The USPSTF and American Cancer Society have different US average-risk schedules, and national programmes also vary. Choose a plan with your clinician using one relevant programme and your history; do not combine all schedules or apply an average-risk rule to a high-risk condition.

Can I use a routine adult diabetes test schedule during pregnancy?

Pregnancy has its own gestational-diabetes testing pathway and thresholds. Tell the service you are pregnant or may be pregnant and follow the antenatal plan. HbA1c measures glucose, not blood pressure, and is not an automatic substitute for the required pregnancy test.

When should I seek care rather than wait for screening?

New lumps, unusual bleeding or discharge, changing skin lesions and new bowel symptoms need clinical assessment. New painful or disturbed vision needs urgent advice; sudden inability to see or sudden severe eye pain needs emergency care. Sudden glaucoma-type eye symptoms also require emergency assessment without waiting for a full set of signs. Do not drive yourself to emergency care. Get immediate help if you cannot keep yourself or another person safe.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
